SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r10.claim: Al-Raghib calls it a Persian loan and notes that Arabic has no simplex noun with this pattern of a medial alif followed by two letters.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r2.claim: The subject of شاء may refer to God, as Ibn Abbas interprets it; most commentators disagree and take it to refer to من.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r3.claim: أحاط بهم سرادقها is an adjectival clause describing نار.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r4.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r4.claim: سرادق can mean anything enclosing something, such as an awning or tent, or an encompassing wall, according to al-Harawi.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r5.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r5.claim: Other explanations identify the سرادق as a chamber around a tent or a canopy stretched over a courtyard.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r6.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r6.claim: A further definition is any house made of felt; Rujba's verse uses سرادق for an extended canopy of glory.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r7.speaker: الشاعر
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r7.claim: An anonymous poem uses بيت مسردق for the house whose roof is described as elephant chests.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r8.speaker: الفرزدق
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r8.claim: Al-Farazdaq's verse uses السرادق for the enclosure left before combat.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r9.speaker: الجواليقي
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#2/r9.claim: Al-Jawaliqi says سرادق is a Persian loan, originally سرادة.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r1.claim: يستغيثوا means to seek help; the yāʾ comes from an original wāw through the same morphological change discussed at 1:5.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r2.claim: The language of answering a plea is verbal matching or wordplay rather than real rescue, since no aid is offered; it may instead be sarcastic.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r3.speaker: قيل
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r3.claim: المهل is explained as the dregs of oil or as melted substances such as copper and lead; with two fatḥas it means deliberation and dignity.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r4.claim: يشوي الوجوه may be a second adjective of ماء, a circumstantial clause from the water, or a circumstantial clause from the prepositional phrase.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:29#3/r5.claim: الشي is cooking by fire without broth accompanying the food being roasted.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r1.claim: الحق can be the predicate of an omitted هذا, referring to the Quran or what was heard.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r2.claim: Alternatively, الحق may be the subject of an omitted verb such as جاء, recoverable from context, though ellipsis is licensed only in specific constructions.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r3.claim: A third parse makes الحق the topic and من ربكم its predicate.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r4.speaker: أبو السمال قعنب
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r4.claim: Abu al-Sammal reads وقل with a rounded imperative lām wherever it occurs, apparently harmonized with qaf.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r5.speaker: أبو السمال قعنب
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r5.claim: He also reads الحق in the accusative; al-Lawamiʿ treats it as an adjective of an implicit verbal noun and attaches من to an implicit جاء.

SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r6.speaker: الحسن والثقفي
SAMIN-DURR:18:29/r6.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Thaqafi read the lām of the imperatives فليؤمن and فليكفر with kasra, its original vowel.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r1.claim: The message brought by Muhammad is the certain truth from God; the choice to believe or disbelieve is a severe threat, and the wrongdoers meant here are those who reject God, His Messenger, and His Book. The fire's enclosure is its wall.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r2.speaker: النبي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r2.claim: The Prophet said Hell's enclosure has four walls, each extending forty years in thickness or distance; Ahmad reports it, and Tirmidhi and Ibn Jarir also transmit it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas defines Hell's enclosure as a wall of fire, in a report from Ibn Jurayj.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r4.speaker: يعلى بن أمية
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#2/r4.claim: Ya'la reports that the Prophet called the sea Hell, then recited this verse when asked how, and swore he would never enter it while alive or be touched by a drop of it.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas describes muhl as thick liquid like the dregs of oil.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r10.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r10.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r10.claim: Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the people of Hell eat Zaqqum when hungry, losing their facial skin, then cry for water and receive muhl so hot that the remaining flesh on their faces is scorched near their mouths.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r2.claim: Mujahid says muhl is like blood and pus.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r3.speaker: عكرمة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r3.claim: Ikrima says muhl is something whose heat has reached its limit.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r4.speaker: آخرون
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r4.claim: Other authorities interpret muhl as anything melted.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r5.speaker: قتادة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r5.claim: Qatada says Ibn Masud melted gold in a trench; once it liquefied and foamed, he called it the closest likeness of muhl.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r6.speaker: الضحاك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r6.claim: Al-Dahhak says Hell's water is black because Hell is black and its people are black.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r7.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r7.claim: These descriptions do not conflict: muhl combines the repulsive traits of being black, foul, thick, and hot.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r8.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r8.speaker: النبي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r8.claim: The Prophet explains that muhl is like oil sediment and that bringing it near makes the face's skin fall into it; Tirmidhi says this route is only known through Rashdin, criticized for memory, while Ahmad transmits it through Ibn Lahi'a.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r9.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r9.speaker: النبي
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p154#3/r9.claim: In a report explaining 14:16–17, Abu Umama says the drink is brought near unwillingly, burns the face and removes the scalp, then cuts the drinker's intestines.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p155/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p155/r1.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p155/r1.claim: The muhl drink is vile and scalding, like the hot water of 47:15 and 88:5; the spring called aniy is intensely hot, as in 55:44.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p155/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p155/r2.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v5p155/r2.claim: The fire is a wretched place to lodge, rest, gather, or seek comfort, like the bad abode and residence described in 25:66.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r1.claim: The revelation delivered about the Cave and related matters is the truth from God, refuting the interlocutors’ claims.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r2.claim: The challenge addresses everyone: faith is accepted even in poverty, while rejection merits disregard and eventual divine vengeance despite worldly wealth or status.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r3.claim: Both faith and unbelief depend on God’s created will: voluntary action requires an intention, and tracing prior intentions infinitely is impossible.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p464/r4.claim: God must create the initiating intention, compelling the act while the human appears to choose; therefore the verse does not support the Muʿtazilites.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r1.claim: The prepared fire is for wrongdoers, meaning unbelievers, and its enclosure surrounds them like a fence around a tent.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r2.claim: Their plea for rain or relief is answered mockingly with molten, thick, intensely hot liquid, compared to thin pitch, melted metal, or oil dregs.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r3.claim: The liquid scorches faces when brought near the mouth, so its effect on the mouth and insides is worse.

BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v4p465/r4.claim: The drink is vile: black, foul-smelling, thick, and hot; the fire is an evil lodging prepared for rest.

DURR-FULL:v5p379/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p379/r10.speaker: سلمان
DURR-FULL:v5p379/r10.claim: Influential men asked the Prophet to exclude poor Muslims such as Salman and Abu Dharr and seat the chiefs instead; revelation of the passage threatened them with Hell.

DURR-FULL:v5p383/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas also reads the invitation to believe or disbelieve as a threat and warning.

DURR-FULL:v5p383/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r11.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r11.claim: Mujahid describes the verse's statement as God's threat that the unbelievers cannot escape.

DURR-FULL:v5p383/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r12.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r12.claim: The canopy surrounding Hell is a wall of fire.

DURR-FULL:v5p383/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r13.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r13.claim: The Prophet described Hell's canopy as four enclosing walls, each forty years in length.

DURR-FULL:v5p383/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r8.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r8.claim: Qatada identifies the truth from one's Lord as the Quran.

DURR-FULL:v5p383/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p383/r9.claim: Ibn Abbas says a person's willing faith or disbelief occurs only as God wills, citing Quran 81:29.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r1.speaker: يعلى بن أمية
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r1.claim: The Prophet said that the sea is part of Hell, then recited the verse about its fiery canopy.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r10.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r10.claim: Mujahid describes molten metal as black pus and blood, like oil sediment.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r11.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r11.claim: Al-Dahhak says the drink is black, as are its people.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r12.speaker: خصيف
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r12.claim: Khasif identifies molten metal as melted copper, hotter than fire.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r13.speaker: الحكم
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r13.claim: Al-Hakam compares the molten drink to melted silver.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r2.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r2.claim: Al-Ahnaf ibn Qays avoided sleeping under a canopy because canopies are mentioned only for Hell's people.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r3.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r3.claim: The Prophet says the drink like molten metal is like the scum of oil; when brought near, the face's skin falls into it.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas describes the molten drink as black like oil sediment.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas calls it a thick water like the dregs of oil.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r6.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r6.claim: Said ibn Jubayr compares the drink to oil dregs.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r7.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r7.claim: Ibn Masud likewise says molten metal is the dregs of oil.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r8.speaker: أبو مالك
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r8.claim: Abu Malik also glosses molten metal as oil sediment.

DURR-FULL:v5p384/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r9.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v5p384/r9.claim: Ibn Masud compared the Hell drink to barely melted gold or silver; it resembled the molten drink, though the latter is hotter.

DURR-FULL:v5p386/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p386/r1.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
DURR-FULL:v5p386/r1.claim: Said ibn Jubayr describes molten metal as being at its most intensely hot.

DURR-FULL:v5p386/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p386/r2.speaker: ابن عمر
DURR-FULL:v5p386/r2.claim: Ibn Umar explains mahl as the sediment or last part of oil.

DURR-FULL:v5p386/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p386/r3.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v5p386/r3.claim: Mujahid glosses a wretched resting place as a gathering place.

DURR-FULL:v5p386/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p386/r4.speaker: قتادة
DURR-FULL:v5p386/r4.claim: Qatada glosses it as a dwelling place.

DURR-FULL:v5p386/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v5p386/r5.speaker: السدي
DURR-FULL:v5p386/r5.claim: Al-Suddi depicts them reclining over boiling water as they drink; irtifaq means a place to recline.

BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r1.speaker: بحر العلوم
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r1.claim: A surādīq is the set of wall panels around a tent, without a roof; Abū Saʿīd transmits the Prophet's description of four dense walls, each a forty-year journey in distance.

BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r10.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r10.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r10.claim: A hadith says the least-punished person in Hell wears two sandals of fire whose heat makes his brain boil.

BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r11.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r11.speaker: مالك بن دينار
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r11.claim: He recounts a laughing, crying child playing in dirt; his self restrained him from greeting while reason urged him to do so. The boy invoked the Prophet's practice, said their souls had known each other in the unseen realm, explained our origin and return to soil and his response to divine punishment and mercy, then urged reflection.

BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r2.speaker: أبو سعيد
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r2.claim: He transmits the Prophet's description of the Fire's enclosure as four dense walls, each the distance of a forty-year journey.

BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r3.claim: When the damned plead for drink, they receive molten metal in place of water; the irony resembles giving a calamity in place of lovers' reproach.

BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r4.claim: A hadith describes the drink as oil sediment, thick and black; when brought near, the face's skin falls away.

BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r5.claim: يشوي means roasting the faces; the drink fails to relieve thirst and instead burns them severely.

BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r6.claim: مرتفقا means a place to recline or dwell; its root is propping an elbow under the cheek, though comfort cannot be meant in Hell.

BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r7.speaker: سعدي المفتي
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r7.claim: He says elbow-resting can express either rest or bewildered sorrow; rest is impossible here but sorrow is possible, so he rejects the alleged wordplay.

BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r8.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r8.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r8.claim: The word means an abode metaphorically, not actual leaning or comfort, since the place is Hell.

BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r9.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r9.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p186#2/r9.claim: Believers should shun wrongdoing and persistent sin; if they fall, repent and occupy themselves with monotheism and remembrance, since the road to Hell is long and its punishment severe.

BURSEVI:v5p186/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p186/r1.claim: The truth comes from God rather than desire; now that revelation has removed excuses, people choose what leads to salvation or ruin.

BURSEVI:v5p186/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186/r2.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
BURSEVI:v5p186/r2.claim: The truth includes glad tidings, warnings, and guidance along paths of happiness and away from destruction.

BURSEVI:v5p186/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186/r3.speaker: الإرشاد
BURSEVI:v5p186/r3.claim: The permission to believe or disbelieve is a threat, not neutral license: God will not expel sincere believers to appease elites after the truth is clear, and human faith neither benefits nor harms God.

BURSEVI:v5p186/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p186/r4.claim: God does not need faith and does not approve unbelief because it harms people, even if He wills it for some; gratitude and faith are pleasing to Him.

BURSEVI:v5p186/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186/r5.speaker: السمرقندي
BURSEVI:v5p186/r5.claim: People who will to believe should direct their capacity and will toward acquiring faith; this shows human choice together with God's creation of acts, a middle position between determinism and free agency, and makes reward and punishment just.

BURSEVI:v5p186/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v5p186/r6.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v5p186/r6.claim: God prepared fire for everyone who wrongs himself by choosing unbelief over belief; its canopy already surrounds them, with the past tense expressing certainty, and سرادق means a tent-like enclosure.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r1.claim: “The truth is from your Lord” has an omitted subject, “this revealed thing is the truth”; “from your Lord” is preferably an emphatic circumstantial phrase.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r2.claim: Alternatively, “the truth” is the subject and “from your Lord” its predicate.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r3.claim: The command to offer belief or disbelief is part of the Prophet’s statement and threatens listeners after establishing the revealed truth’s binding authority.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r4.claim: The threat shows the Prophet does not depend on the elite’s promised conversion, which they conditioned on expelling the believers.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r5.speaker: الكشف
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r5.claim: Al-Kashf favors the omitted subject because it joins the thought tightly to the preceding command to remain with sincere worshippers and ignore worldly adornment.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r6.claim: Zamakhshari favors construing the preceding phrase with an omitted subject rather than making الحق the subject.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r7.claim: Under either construction, some identify the truth as the Qur’an, the view transmitted from Muqatil.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r8.speaker: الضحاك
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r8.claim: Al-Dahhak identifies the truth as divine unity.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r9.speaker: الكرماني
ALUSI-FULL:v15p265#2/r9.claim: Al-Kirmani identifies it as Islam and the Qur’an.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r1.speaker: مكي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r1.claim: Makki says الحق means that guidance and abandonment come from God, who guides or leaves whom He wills; the author dismisses this interpretation.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r10.speaker: السدي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r10.claim: Al-Suddi says this verse was abrogated by the statement that people will only will what God wills; the author says that is false if meant literally.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r11.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r11.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reportedly glosses the choices as those God wills to believe or disbelieve.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r2.claim: Another parsing makes the belief-or-disbelief clause a divine threat following the Prophet’s commanded declaration, rather than part of that declaration.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r3.claim: On either parsing, this is not a literal command granting an ethically neutral choice to believe or disbelieve.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r4.speaker: الخفاجي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r4.claim: Al-Khafaji calls the command to disbelieve a metaphor for abandonment and indifference, like telling someone to do as they please.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r5.speaker: كثير
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r5.claim: Kathir’s verse, “Do us wrong or treat us well; no blame,” illustrates the rhetorical show of indifference.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r6.speaker: المعتزلة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r6.claim: Muʿtazilites infer human independence because belief and unbelief are made contingent on the human chooser’s will.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r7.speaker: الأشاعرة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r7.claim: The author replies that even if human will produces acts, it itself depends on God’s will, so independence fails; this is the Ashʿari position of humans compelled in the form of choosers.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r8.speaker: الغزالي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r8.claim: Al-Ghazali argues that although one feels able to act or refrain at will, one does not choose whether the will itself arises; both will and action follow necessarily.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p266/r9.claim: Some establish non-independence from the scriptural dependence of human will on God alone, without the contested regress argument.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r1.speaker: الحسن وعيسى الثقفي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r1.claim: Al-Hasan and ʿIsa al-Thaqafi read both imperative lām particles with kasra.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r10.speaker: القاضي الماوردي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r10.claim: Al-Mawardi says the surrounding sea will become fire on the Day of Resurrection and encircle them.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r11.speaker: يلعى بن أمية
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r11.claim: A report from Yala ibn Umayya says the Prophet called the sea part of Hell and recited this verse; the source notes that Ibn Abi Hatim authenticated it.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r12.speaker: الراغب
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r12.claim: Raghib says سرادق is a Persian loanword, but his claim that its consonant pattern is unattested in Arabic is refuted by several Arabic examples.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r13.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r13.claim: Proposed Persian sources include سرايرده, “covering of the court,” and سراطاق, “arch of the court”; Abu Hayyan instead cites سرداد, meaning vestibule.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r14.speaker: سيبويه
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r14.claim: The masculine loanword takes a sound feminine plural, سرادقات; lexicographers define it as anything enclosing a place or shelter.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r15.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r15.claim: The appeal for help is contextualized as thirst by the water that follows, though it may concern every kind of torment.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r16.speaker: ابن عباس وابن جبير
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r16.claim: They describe the molten drink as thick liquid like the dregs of oil.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r17.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r17.claim: A Prophetic report likens the drink to oil dregs and says that when brought near, the face’s skin falls into it.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r18.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r18.speaker: غير واحد
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r18.claim: Other authorities identify the drink as molten substances from the earth or molten copper.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r19.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r19.speaker: ابن مسعود
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r19.claim: Ibn Masʿud compares molten gold and silver to the drink’s appearance, while stressing that Hell’s drink is much hotter.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r2.claim: The “wrongdoers” are those who disbelieve after the truth comes from God; naming them wrongdoers underscores their choice as transgression.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r20.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r20.speaker: مجاهد
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r20.claim: Mujahid identifies the drink as pus and black blood; another view calls it a kind of tar.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r21.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r21.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r21.claim: The promise that they will be given drink is sarcastic understatement, illustrated by Bishr ibn Abi Hazim’s line about being compensated with slaughter.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r22.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r22.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r22.claim: The extreme heat will roast their faces and strip their skin; “faces” most likely means the actual facial organs, though it may stand for whole bodies.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r23.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r23.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r23.claim: يشوي الوجوه can modify the water as a second adjective or circumstantial clause, or be a circumstantial clause from the molten drink.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r3.claim: The prepared Fire either explains the threatening choice or reinforces the divine threat if the choice clause is itself from God.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r4.claim: أعتدنا means “prepared,” from عتاد, or derives from أعددنا with one د replaced by ت.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r5.claim: The Fire’s spreading flames around the unbelievers are likened to a tent enclosure; سرادق is a metaphor for its enveloping barrier.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r6.claim: Other explanations of سرادق include a tent’s surrounding curtain or rising smoke that encircles something; both are figurative here.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r7.speaker: قتادة
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r7.claim: Qatada reportedly interprets the enclosure as the combination of flame and smoke.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the enclosure is a wall of fire.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r9.speaker: الكلبي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267#2/r9.claim: Al-Kalbi describes it as a neck emerging from the Fire and encircling the unbelievers.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r1.claim: Alusi cites the Ibn ʿAbbas report from Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r2.claim: If the report is sound, Alusi says it explains human choices as accordant with God’s will rather than changing the grammatical subject.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r3.claim: Grammatically the subject is “whoever”; if Ibn ʿAbbas’s report is sound, it explains that the human chooser’s will accords with God’s, as the verse’s ending confirms.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r4.speaker: أبو السمال قعنب
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r4.claim: Abu al-Sammal reads قل الحق with a fatḥa on the lām; Abu Hatim calls this poor Arabic.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r5.speaker: أبو السمال قعنب
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r5.claim: He is also reported to read the lām with ḍamma, apparently harmonizing it with the preceding قاف.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r6.speaker: أبو السمال قعنب
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r6.claim: He also reads الحق in the accusative, parsed as though the command said “speak the true statement.”

ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p267/r7.claim: من ربكم is variously parsed as a circumstantial phrase or as an adjective, with the adjectival analysis raising a grammatical question.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r1.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r1.claim: Some place يشوي الوجوه circumstantially with the hidden pronoun in كالمهل, but al-Khafaji objects that the particle is not an adjective able to contain a pronoun.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r10.speaker: ابن عطاء
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r10.claim: Ibn ʿAta glosses it as a place of settlement.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r11.speaker: العتبي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r11.claim: Al-ʿUtbi glosses it as a gathering place.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r12.speaker: مجاهد
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r12.claim: Mujahid explains it as a place where people meet and associate; the author rejects al-Tabari’s denial that this sense is possible.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r2.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r2.claim: Abu ʿAli al-Farisi likewise says it is difficult to make ذؤابتي the subject of كـ in the poetic comparison to a partridge’s nest.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r3.claim: “How wretched a drink” refers to the water they receive, and “how evil a resting place” refers to the Fire.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r4.speaker: أبو عبيدة والسدي
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r4.claim: Abu ʿUbayda and al-Suddi explain مرتفقا as a place or posture for leaning on the elbow.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r5.claim: The word derives from leaning on the arm’s elbow; مرتفقا may be a place noun used as a specification.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r6.claim: Zamakhshari calls مرتفقا a contrastive echo of “a good resting place” in 18:31, since Hell offers neither rest nor reclining.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r7.speaker: الكشف
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r7.claim: Al-Kashf argues reclining can express grief as well as comfort, so the phrase might be literal.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r8.claim: The author says punishment would occupy them too fully for literal reclining, so the phrase is mockery or a metonym for their lack of comfort.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r9.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI-FULL:v15p268/r9.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas interprets مرتفقا as a dwelling place; Qatada gives the same general sense.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p269/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p269/r1.speaker: ابن الأنباري
ALUSI-FULL:v15p269/r1.claim: Ibn al-Anbari reads the phrase as saying Hell is a terrible destination for someone seeking relief, since its seeker finds none.

ALUSI-FULL:v15p269/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v15p269/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v15p269/r2.claim: Some parse مرتفقا as a verbal noun meaning reclining or seeking repose.

ELMALILI:18:27-31/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:18:27-31/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:18:27-31/r3.claim: The torment passage is rendered as scalding water that chars faces and a wretched drink and “kurultay” (gathering place).

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r1.claim: After rejecting the polytheists’ proposals, the Prophet must state plainly that he follows and delivers God’s truth without compromise or selective acceptance; belief and disbelief remain their choice.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r2.claim: Al-ḥaqq is the predicate of an omitted ‘this is’; calling God ‘your Lord’ recalls the obligation to affirm His oneness.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r3.claim: The paired imperatives ‘believe’ and ‘disbelieve’ express a threat through apparent equal choice; belief comes first because it is desired.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r4.claim: The subject of both acts is the relative ‘whoever’; the futures include continuing one’s current state, since resolving to continue renews the act.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r5.claim: The fire warning answers the question raised by leaving belief to their choice; the ‘wrongdoers’ are polytheists, as at 31:13, and the indefinite fire magnifies the threat.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r6.claim: Sarādiq may mean a tent or the surrounding barrier that may be cloth, leather, or a trench; the word is Persian in origin, sarāṭāq.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p307#2/r7.claim: The fire is imagined as a house enclosed by a pavilion, intensifying its confinement; using a luxury dwelling’s canopy for punishment is a sarcastic metaphor.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r1.claim: Their plea for help includes relief from the fire’s heat and drink for thirst, as in 7:50; the ‘help’ ironically intensifies what they seek to escape.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r2.claim: Muhl most plausibly means oil sediment, whose heat feeds the flames; its darkness and extreme temperature worsen the burning, as at 70:8.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r3.claim: The comparison emphasizes the liquid’s blackness and intense heat; it brings no cooling and instead burns faces, as at 23:104.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r4.claim: The clause about scorching faces starts a new statement; the face suffers most from fire’s heat.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r5.claim: ‘Wretched drink’ independently condemns the liquid; the omitted object is ‘that water,’ contrasted with the praised cool bath and drink at 38:42.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r6.claim: ‘How evil a resting place’ is a new condemnation of the fire itself; murtfaq means a place of rest or support, derived through the elbow joint used for leaning.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p308/r7.claim: Calling hell a resting place is sarcastic, like calling the torment ‘help’ and describing the fire as a pavilion-surrounded home.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p309/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p309/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v15p309/r1.claim: Sāʾa functions like biʾsa as a verb of dispraise; murtfaqan is its specification, while the target of blame is omitted as with ‘wretched drink.’

TABATABAI:18:28-29/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:28-29/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:28-29/r4.claim: The command to tell people that truth is from their Lord continues the Prophet’s duties: recite revelation, remain with poor believers, and simply announce the truth while people choose.

TABATABAI:18:28-29/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:28-29/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:28-29/r5.claim: “Whoever wills, let him believe” is God’s address to the Prophet, not part of the quoted command; it presents a formal choice whose threat is made clear by the prepared punishment.

TABATABAI:18:28-29/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:28-29/r6.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:28-29/r6.claim: The fire for wrongdoers explains why the Prophet need not press them: the choice carries its own deterrent and consequence, while benefit or harm returns to them.

TABATABAI:18:28-29/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:28-29/r7.speaker: المجمع
TABATABAI:18:28-29/r7.claim: Al-Majmaʿ defines sarādiq as an enclosing tent-cloth, muhl as oil dregs or molten copper, murtafaq as a leaning place, and shawā as cooking or ripening.

TABATABAI:18:29-31/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:29-31/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:29-31/r1.claim: Calling the punished people “wrongdoers” rather than “disbelievers” identifies the punishment as due to injustice; 7:45 describes them as those who bar God’s path, distort it, and deny the Hereafter.

TABATABAI:18:29-31/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:29-31/r6.speaker: سلمان
TABATABAI:18:29-31/r6.claim: Salman reports that influential converts, including ʿUyayna ibn Badr and al-Aqraʿ ibn Ḥābis, asked the Prophet to remove shabby poor Muslims such as Salman and Abū Dharr; the passage then warned them of fire.

TABATABAI:18:29-31/r7.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:29-31/r7.speaker: author
TABATABAI:18:29-31/r7.claim: Al-Qummī gives a similar report naming only ʿUyayna ibn al-Ḥuṣayn; its Medina setting and related reports conflict with the passage’s Meccan context.

TABATABAI:18:29/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:29/r2.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:29/r2.claim: Al-ʿAyyāshī reports that the phrase “whoever wills, let him believe or disbelieve” is a threat.

TABATABAI:18:29/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:29/r3.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:29/r3.claim: A report from al-Bāqir interprets “the truth is from your Lord” as concerning allegiance to ʿAlī; the author classifies it as an application of the verse.

TABATABAI:18:29/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:29/r4.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
TABATABAI:18:29/r4.claim: A report from Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī explains the liquid like molten metal as oil dregs; when brought near, facial skin falls into it.

TABATABAI:18:29/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:29/r5.speaker: القمي
TABATABAI:18:29/r5.claim: Al-Qummī glosses muhl as the sediment left at the bottom of oil.

TABATABAI:18:29/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:18:29/r6.speaker: أبو عبد الله عليه السلام
TABATABAI:18:29/r6.claim: Ibn Sinān reports al-Ṣādiq’s reminder that humans are hollow and need food and drink, linking it to the drink that scorches faces in 18:29.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The next section resumes the surah's opening: after the cave story showed God helping those who serve His cause, the Prophet is told to keep reciting, direct guidance to poor companions, disregard wealthy opponents, and leave them their choice and fate.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The Prophet should state plainly that this is the truth from his Lord rather than pamper the affluent opponents.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Marja' is a place to lean on; Islahi translates it more broadly as an abode.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: The verb yeshwi means to fry and muhl means molten brass, underscoring the water's intense heat.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Descriptions of Paradise and Hell belong to the mutashābihāt: parables make the unseen intelligible, while God alone knows their actual form.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-4-surah-yunus-10-sur.claim: Qur’anic descriptions use what Arabs know and value, since a parable works only when its audience understands its purport.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:29/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:29/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:29/r1.claim: The divine message addresses everyone equally regardless of status; each person may believe or disbelieve and bears the resulting benefit or harm, with no coercion or expulsion of sincere poor believers.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:29/r2.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:29/r2.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:29/r2.claim: The verse grounds religious freedom and indicates that unbelievers retain basic human rights in this world.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:29/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:29/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:18:29/r3.claim: People are given reason and will to distinguish truth from falsehood; forcing guidance would conflict with responsibility and reward, and persistent falsehood darkens the heart; see 6:39, 107, and 111 on divine will.

STUDYQURAN:18:29/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r1.claim: The verse is also associated with the incident in verse 28, when prominent Makkans sought to exclude poor believers.

STUDYQURAN:18:29/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r10.claim: Faces stand for persons as a whole in descriptions of punishment, rather than only the body part.

STUDYQURAN:18:29/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r2.claim: “Believe or disbelieve” is a warning, not permission to reject; the Prophet declares truth but does not determine acceptance, which ultimately belongs to God.

STUDYQURAN:18:29/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r3.speaker: commentators
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r3.claim: One view says acceptance or rejection ultimately lies with God.

STUDYQURAN:18:29/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r4.speaker: commentators
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r4.claim: Another view frames the choice from the human perspective: each person chooses whether to follow truth or turn away.

STUDYQURAN:18:29/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r5.claim: The warning is confirmed by the Hell punishment described in the latter half of the verse.

STUDYQURAN:18:29/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r6.claim: The canopies of Fire surround wrongdoers on every side, above and below.

STUDYQURAN:18:29/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r7.claim: The molten-like liquid may be poured on Hell’s inhabitants or made them drink; here it is both poured on them and an evil drink.

STUDYQURAN:18:29/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r8.speaker: some commentators
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r8.claim: Some picture a wall of water poured into Hell; when its inhabitants seek relief by drinking, its heat burns their faces.

STUDYQURAN:18:29/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:18:29/r9.claim: Hell’s boiling and freezing drinks contrast with the Garden’s pleasant drinks.
